lead: For alloys, pressure is fixed at 1 atm, so the phase rule loses one variable. The reduced phase rule F = C − P + 1 counts the intensive degrees of freedom left. The lead–silver system is the standard simple eutectic: two metals, no compound, one lowest melting point. Foundries use such diagrams to choose pouring temperatures; solder and fuse alloys sit near eutectics.
prereq: You need phase rule terms and one-component diagrams.

blocks.text: At constant pressure, the ordinary phase rule F = C − P + 2 becomes F = C − P + 1. C is the number of components; P is the number of phases; F is the number of intensive variables (temperature, composition) you can change without losing a phase. Fixing pressure removes one degree of freedom.

blocks.where: F is the reduced degrees of freedom; C is the number of components (2 for Pb and Ag); P is the number of phases present.

blocks.text: For Pb–Ag, C = 2. One liquid phase gives P = 1, so F = 2: temperature and composition may change. Two phases give F = 1. Three phases give F = 0. At zero freedom the temperature and all phase compositions are fixed; this is the eutectic point.

The diagram plots temperature T in °C against mass% Ag. Pure Pb melts at 327 °C; pure Ag at 961 °C. The two liquidus lines meet at the eutectic: 303 °C and 2.5 mass% Ag. Above the liquidus is one liquid. Left of 2.5% is primary Pb plus liquid; right is primary Ag plus liquid. Below 303 °C are two solids, Pb and Ag.

At the eutectic, liquid ↔ solid Pb + solid Ag. A tie line at 303 °C joins the two solid compositions (pure Pb and pure Ag) and the liquid at 2.5% Ag. The lever rule gives the amount of each phase: mass of phase = (opposite segment length ÷ total tie-line length) × total mass.
Alloys below 2.5% Ag are hypo-eutectic; above are hyper-eutectic. A 5% Ag alloy is hyper-eutectic, so primary Ag appears first on cooling.

A eutectic alloy cools with one flat halt at 303 °C until all liquid freezes; F = 0. An off-eutectic alloy first shows a break at its liquidus, where one solid appears and F = 1. It then reaches 303 °C and halts at F = 0. After freezing, temperature falls again.

If the two components form a compound that melts congruently, the diagram has a peak at the compound's composition. Zn–Mg is one example. Only a few universities teach this diagram; compound details belong to a materials course.

examples.question: An alloy is made from 5.0 g Ag and 95.0 g Pb. Find mass% Ag, classify it, F at the eutectic with liquid and both solids, and F at 400 °C in the liquid region.
steps: Eutectic is 2.5 mass% Ag; 5.0% > 2.5%, so hyper-eutectic.
At eutectic: P = 3 (liquid, solid Pb, solid Ag), C = 2. F = 2 − 3 + 1 = 0.
examples.answer: The alloy is 5.0 mass% Ag, hyper-eutectic; F = 0 at the eutectic and F = 2 at 400 °C in the liquid.
examples.check:
mass_ag = 5.0
mass_pb = 95.0
total = mass_ag + mass_pb
pct_ag = 100 * mass_ag / total
C = 2
P_eut = 3
F_eut = C - P_eut + 1
P_liq = 1
F_liq = C - P_liq + 1
print(pct_ag)
print(F_eut)
print(F_liq)

traps: Never use F = C − P + 2 when pressure is fixed; the reduced rule is F = C − P + 1.
The eutectic is a mixture of two solids, not a compound.
At the eutectic, P = 3 (liquid + solid Pb + solid Ag), so F = 0.
Mass% and mole% are different; this diagram uses mass% Ag.
F = 0 does not mean nothing changes; it means no intensive variable can change without losing a phase.
